Arabic; he mixes English and Arabic and makes learner mistakes. Amal is his teacher (native Levantine). A speech engine
wrote the transcript below; it often MISHEARS Medi's Arabic as a different Arabic word, or as English look-alike words.

The audio clip is ONLY Medi's microphone for the target line. Context (engine text of the lines around it; seconds
before (-) / after (+) the target line):
-35.2 s Amal: like we haven't checked all of it so you can also review it for next time.
-29.8 s Medi: Yeah. So my, my intention wasn't to have it show you all my results, but I think it's showing you anytime I look at a flashcard, I think it's showing you the results.
-22.0 s Amal: Yeah. [تضحك]
-19.1 s Medi: So that's fine. You can see them.
-16.8 s Amal: That's cool.
-14.3 s Medi: And you can see if I, if I finish the set too, so...
-8.9 s Amal: [تضحك] I hope that's a motivation. But today you were kind of distracted so next time
-8.2 s Medi: And now I can't do it right before the lesson or you'll know that I'm procrastinating. [laughs] Yeah.
+3.1 s Amal: drink coffee. [تضحك] يلا. يعطيك العافية.
+6.7 s Medi: Yeah. Okay. Shukran. Alayfiqi. Bashufik. Bye
+11.6 s Amal: بشوفك. سلام. باي.
Amal's typed chat lines near this moment (she often types the sentence Medi was trying to say, in her Arabizi; her typed
version may be CORRECTED, so it shows what he meant, not always what he said): (none)

TARGET: Medi's line that the engine wrote as: «[laughs] Okay, I'll try.».

Sound-alike words the engine keeps swapping in Medi's Arabic - when you hear one of a group, consider the others and pick by the word after it:
- على (3ala = on / at (3ala el-3ashrah = at ten)) / إلى (ila = to (MSA; Medi rarely means it - usually 3ala or la-)) / الله (allah = God (in a set phrase: inshallah, wallah, el-7amdellah)) / ألا (alla = unless / isn't it (rare for Medi)) / لـ (la- = to / for (the dialect 'to')). Medi says 3ala for 'on/at' far more than ila; 'allah' only inside inshallah / wallah / 7amdellah. Decide by the noun after it.
- العشرة (el-3ashrah = ten (the hour ten)) / العشاء (el-3asha = dinner / the evening prayer) / عشر (3asher = ten (before a noun: 3asher da2aaye2)). after 3ala + a time word it is the hour (el-3ashrah); after 'akal / 3azam' it is dinner (el-3asha).
- متشجع (mitshajje3 = motivated) / شجاع (shuja3 = brave) / متحمس (mit7ammes = excited). Medi reaches for 'motivated' and says shuja3 (brave); Amal recasts mitshajje3.
- صحيت (s7eet = I woke up) / سمعت (sme3et = I heard). with met2a55ar / el-subu7 it is 'woke up'.

How to use the context (general, true of these lessons):
- Medi often REPEATS Amal's previous sentence with small changes (her "you woke up late" -> his "I woke up late"): if his
  line sounds like hers, expect her words in it.
- An answer must fit the question just before it (asked "what time?", he answers with a time).
- Amal's next reaction shows what she heard: if she only fixes one small piece, the rest was right as she heard it.
- The engine prefers common words; a common word that makes the sentence nonsense is probably a mishearing.
- Amal's correction AFTER his line is what he should have said, not what he said: never put her fix into his line.

Write exactly what MEDI said in the target line:
- keep his mistakes, wrong words, wrong endings, wrong vowels and false starts exactly as he said them (do NOT correct his Arabic);
- fix only what the engine misheard;
- if he spoke English, write the English.
Answer JSON only: {"arabic": "his words in Arabic script (English words stay English)", "arabizi": "his words in Latin letters with 2 3 5 6 7 8 9 for ء ع خ ط ح غ ص", "engine_was_wrong": true|false, "changes": [{"engine": "...", "said": "..."}], "confidence": "high"|"medium"|"low", "why": "one short reason"}
